metadata.title: Fermi's Golden Rule — Riff on the Viz

beats.narration_text: Ciao, Liam — in for Bear. A physics student asks: build me a visualization of Fermi's Golden Rule. Claude hands one back. We are not here to learn the physics — we are here to judge whether this visualization earns it.

props.command: Hey Claude, write me a visualization for Fermi's Golden Rule — transition probability.

beats.narration_text: Here is what loaded. Title: Fermi's Golden Rule — Transition Probability. The formula is in the subtitle. Two panels: top shows P of Omega and t versus detuning Omega — a red sinc-squared curve with a blue dashed envelope. Bottom shows on-resonance probability versus time — a red parabola, a gray dashed golden-rule rate line, and a dotted breakdown marker at P equals one. Two sliders: TIME T from zero-point-one to twenty, and DENSITY OF STATES rho from zero-point-one to ten. A toggle switches the top panel between probability and rate. That is the layout. No judgment yet.

Drag the time slider. Two things happen at once in the top panel: the sinc-squared peak grows — proportional to t-squared — and it narrows — the first zero moves inward at two-pi over t. At t equals two, a broad hill. At t equals ten, a sharp spike that has just hit P equals one — the perturbation theory limit. At t equals twenty, a needle. That convergence — broad function collapsing toward a delta spike at zero detuning — is the mathematical origin of the golden rule. The sweep IS the argument.

Three things this visualization earns. First: the two-panel layout. Top gives the detuning-space picture; bottom gives the time-domain picture. Neither alone closes the argument. Both together do — and the red circle marker links them: one position in the bottom panel corresponds to exactly the peak height shown in the top panel. Second: the live first-zero annotation. As you drag, the text updates — First zero: Omega equals plus-or-minus two-pi over t equals this number right now. That number is the argument. Watching it shrink is what no static textbook figure can provide. Third: the physics-checks console. P1 PASS, P2 PASS, P3 PASS. A visualization that proves its own correctness in front of the student is not common.

Three things to fix. First: the rho slider does nothing visible to the top panel and the layout says nothing about why. A student moves rho, the sinc-squared curve does not move, and there is no tooltip, no label, no annotation explaining that rho enters only in the rate integral — not in P of Omega and t. It looks like a broken control. One sentence under the slider fixes it. Second: W means two different things on the same screen. In rate mode, the top panel labels the y-axis W of Omega and t equals P over t. The bottom panel and console display W equals two-pi vertical-bar V vertical-bar squared rho — the golden-rule scalar. Same letter, incompatible quantities. Students will conflate them. Third: the code uses d3.curveBasis — B-spline smoothing — on the sinc-squared path. At large t the sidelobes are physically sharp. Smoothing blunts them. The sidelobes are the argument for energy selectivity; blunting them blunts the lesson.

Let's recap with Claude. The two-panel layout earns the golden rule argument — no single graph does that. The rho slider's silence needs one label to become a physics lesson, not a UI mystery. d3.curveBasis blunts sidelobes that carry the energy-selectivity proof — swap in curveLinear. Use this viz immediately after the algebra, before touching density of states.

artifactLines: Two-panel design — both panels needed to close the argument
ρ slider silence needs one label: ρ enters only the rate integral
Use after the algebra, before touching density of states

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take the Fermi's Golden Rule simulation and make three targeted improvements. One: add a one-sentence note below the rho slider — quote, rho enters only the rate integral, not P of Omega and t — so its silence is a physics statement. Two: in the rate-mode toggle, rename the bottom-panel quantity from W to Gamma-GR to break the W notation collision with the top panel. Three: change d3.curveBasis to d3.curveLinear on the sinc-squared path so the sidelobes at large t are geometrically honest. Keep the two-panel layout, the live annotations, and the physics-checks console unchanged. Deliver a single self-contained HTML file.
